narration: The dataset (1200 rows × 24 cols) is not ready for training as-is. Missingness is widespread: the categorical block is the worst offender, with industry carrying the most missing data (missing_count 265, missing_pct 0.22083333333333333, cardinality 31), followed by language (missing_count 234, missing_pct 0.195, cardinality 27), payment_method (missing_count 167, missing_pct 0.13916666666666666, cardinality 23) and acquisition_channel (missing_count 152, missing_pct 0.12666666666666668, cardinality 19); device_type (missing_count 100, missing_pct 0.08333333333333333) and plan_tier also have gaps. Numeric columns also need attention: balance (missing_count 102, missing_pct 0.085) and referral_count (missing_count 103, missing_pct 0.08583333333333333) top the numeric missing list, with support_tickets (missing_pct 0.0825), basket_size (missing_pct 0.07833333333333334) and tenure_months (missing_pct 0.06) close behind. Sentinels are clearly present: balance, session_minutes and discount_rate all share max = 9999.0 while their means are 126.69, 127.37 and 130.68 versus medians near 54-62, so those extreme values must be recoded as missing or clipped before any model sees them. Outliers flagged by IQR (up to 15) and z-score counts also appear across several numeric columns. Finally, the target is a clean binary label (cardinality 2) with mild imbalance (~69/31), which is manageable. Recommend an explicit per-column imputation/missing-indicator strategy for the high-missing categoricals, sentinel treatment for 9999 values, and outlier handling before training.

The dataset (1200 rows x 24 cols) is a binary classification task on `target` (cardinality 2, roughly 69/31 split), but it is not yet train-ready — cleaning is required before modeling.

Missingness is the primary issue and is concentrated in the categorical block, not the numerics. The column carrying the most missing data is `industry` (missing_count 265, missing_pct 0.22083333333333333, cardinality 31), followed by `language` (missing_count 234, missing_pct 0.195, cardinality 27), `payment_method` (missing_count 167, missing_pct 0.13916666666666666, cardinality 23), `acquisition_channel` (missing_count 152, missing_pct 0.12666666666666668, cardinality 19) and `device_type` (missing_count 100, missing_pct 0.08333333333333333, cardinality 15). These are all high-cardinality categoricals with double-digit missing rates, so naive mode imputation would distort them — imputation needs its own strategy (e.g. an explicit "unknown" level, or dropping columns past a threshold). Numeric missingness is milder, topping out at `balance` (missing_pct 0.085) with `referral_count` at 0.08583333333333333 and `support_tickets` at 0.0825; none of the numeric columns exceed ~9% missing.

A second, more serious problem is corrupted value ranges. Three numeric columns share a sentinel-like max of 9999.0 — `balance` (max 9999.0), `session_minutes` (max 9999.0) and `discount_rate` (max 9999.0) — while their means are near 126.7, 127.4 and 130.7 respectively and their standard deviations are enormous (`balance` std 846.2405882223285, `session_minutes` std 828.4903130487685, `discount_rate` std 824.5927764680694). A max that is roughly 100x the median for all three strongly suggests a placeholder/error code rather than real measurements, and it inflates the outlier tallies (`balance` iqr_count 11 / z_score_count 8, `session_minutes` iqr_count 15 / z_score_count 8, `discount_rate` iqr_count 15 / z_score_count 8). These need to be treated as missing or excluded.

Clean columns exist as anchors: `signup_date` (missing_pct 0.0), `is_active` (missing_pct 0.0), plus `credit_score` and `page_views` at 0.0 missing.

Verdict: needs_cleaning — resolve the categorical missingness (starting with `industry`), decide the fate of the 9999.0 sentinel values in `balance`/`session_minutes`/`discount_rate`, then re-profile. Recommended checks: impute or drop high-cardinality categoricals with >10% missing; treat 9999.0 as missing in the three flagged numerics; re-examine class balance after dropping the corrupted rows.

The dataset is 1200 rows x 24 columns with a binary target (cardinality 2) and a mild class imbalance (about 31% positive). It is not ready to train as-is, for three reasons.

1) Missingness. Several catetorical columns lose a meaningful share of their rows: industry has missing_pct 0.22083333333333333 (missing_count 265), language 0.195 (234), payment_method 0.13916666666666666 (167), acquisition_channel 0.12666666666666668 (152), and device_type 0.08333333333333333 (100). The highest-missing column is industry at 22.1% missing — above the 20% threshold at which I would question whether the column is worth imputing at all. On the numeric side, referral_count is missing 0.08583333333333333 (103 rows) and balance 0.085 (102 rows). None reach 50%, so imputation is viable, but dropping rows would discard roughly a quarter of the data if done naively across columns.

2) Cardinality. The heavily-missing columns are also high-cardinality: industry has cardinality 31, language 27, payment_method 23, acquisition_channel 19. Combined with 12-22% missingness, imputation will be unreliable — a missing industry value cannot be confidently recovered from the other features.

3) Sentinels. balance, session_minutes, and discount_rate each report max 9999.0, far beyond their q75 values (63.17, 66.60, 70.05 respectively) and each shows z_score_count 8. These look like placeholder/sentinel values rather than real measurements, so they should be recoded to null before imputing — otherwise imputation and scaling will be skewed.

Recommended path: treat the 9999 codes as missing, choose an explicit strategy for the >10% missing categorical columns (possibly drop industry/language), and impute the low-missing numerics. Confidence is medium because the profile shows no row-level values or leakage evidence.
